(p-172)Surat al-Sharh (The Expansion)

Meccan; it has eight verses.

﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ Since the breast (al-sadr) is the locus of the states of the soul (al-nafs) and the storehouse of its inner secrets, consisting of knowledge, perceptions, faculties (malakat) and volitions, and other things, Allah expressed its expansion (sharh) as widening the scope of its activities by strengthening it with the holy power (al-quwwah al-qudsiyyah) and adorning it with human perfections (al-kamalat al-insiyyah). That is: Did We not make it spacious until it encompassed the two worlds, the unseen (al-ghayb) and the visible (al-shahadah), and combined the two faculties of receiving (al-istifadah) and giving (al-ifadah)? So the attachment to physical relations did not prevent you from drawing on the lights of the spiritual faculties, and the preoccupation with the interests of creation did not hinder you from being absorbed in the affairs of the Real (al-Haqq).

It has also been said that what is meant is what is narrated: "Gabriel came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his childhood, or on the Day of the Covenant, and extracted his heart, washed it, and then filled it with faith and knowledge." Perhaps this is an illustration of what has been mentioned, or a physical model (unmudhaj jismani) of what will later appear to him (upon him be blessings and peace) of spiritual perfection. The expression of the affirmation of the expansion (thubut al-sharh) by way of a rhetorical interrogative of its negation is to indicate that its establishment is so evident that no one can answer it except with "Yes" (bala). The addition of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur), together with its placement between the verb and its object, is to indicate from the very beginning that the expansion is among his (upon him be blessings and peace) benefits and interests, hastening to bring joy into his heart (upon him be blessings and peace), and arousing his anticipation for what follows, so that it may settle most firmly in him at the time of its arrival.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ is an ʿatf (coordination, conjunction) upon what was indicated by the implied meaning (mudlul) of the preceding clause (jumla), as if it were said: "We expanded your breast, and We removed..." etc. "ʿAnka" (from you) is related to (mutaʿalliq bi) "waḍaʿnā" (We removed). Its placement before the explicit object (mafʿul sarih), although its proper place is after it, is due to the purpose mentioned just before, namely hastening the delight and creating anticipation for what is delayed, and because its description (wasf) is somewhat lengthy, so the prepositional phrase (jarr wa majrur) is delayed after it, for the same purpose mentioned just before, of hastening. That is: We lifted from you your heavy load.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 94, verse 3:

﴿Who had weighed down your back﴾. That is: He caused it to be likened to the nagid (naqid), which is the sound of breaking apart and separating, as is heard from a saddle-pack about to break apart from the weight of the load. His condition, peace and blessings be upon him, was likened to this in respect of what burdened him and distressed him of his lapses before prophethood, or of his not having full knowledge of the details of the rulings and laws, or of his extreme eagerness for the conversion of the obstinate ones among his people, his longing for them, and his placing himself in distress over their forgiveness and the teaching of the laws, and his paving the way for his excuse after he had conveyed and exerted himself to the utmost. It was also read "wa-hatatna" and "halalna" in place of "wada'na" (﴿We removed﴾ and ﴿We lifted﴾), and it was read "wa-halalna 'anka wizrak" (﴿And We lifted from you your burden﴾).

﴿And We raised high for you your remembrance﴾ through the title of prophethood and its rulings, to a degree of elevation beyond measure. His name was joined with the name of Allah the Exalted in the testimony of faith (*shahada*), in the call to prayer (*adhan*), and in the call immediately before the prayer (*iqama*). He made obedience to him to be obedience to Him, the Exalted. He sent blessings upon him, He and His angels, and commanded the believers to invoke blessings upon him. He was named "Messenger of Allah" and "Prophet of Allah." The discussion regarding the conjunction (*'atf*) and the addition of "لَكَ" (*laka*) is as has passed.

The words of Allah Most High, ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, are a confirmation of what precedes them, and His promise is a generous one: the easing of every difficulty for him, peace and blessings be upon him, and for the believers. It is as if it were said: We have bestowed upon you what We have bestowed of great blessings; so be confident in the grace and kindness of Allah Most High, for indeed with hardship comes ease, abundant ease. And in His saying "with" (maʿa) there is an indication of the utmost swiftness in the arrival of ease, as if it accompanies the hardship.

Verse 6: "Indeed, with hardship comes ease" (inna ma'a al-'usri yusra). This is a repetition for emphasis (taktir li'l-ta'kid), or a separate promise (ʿidah mustaʾnafah) that hardship is accompanied by another ease, such as the reward of the Hereafter. It is like your saying: "Indeed, the fasting person has two joys: a joy for the fasting person" — that is, a joy at the time of breaking the fast and a joy at meeting the Lord. On this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hardship will never overcome two eases." For when a definite noun (al-ma'rifah) is repeated, the second is the very same as the first, whether it is a previously known referent (ma'hud) or a generic (jins). As for an indefinite noun (al-munakkar), it may be intended that the second is a different individual from what was intended by the first.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 94, verse 7:**

﴿So when you are free﴾, i.e., from conveying (the message) (al-tabligh). It is also said: from fighting (al-ghazw).

﴿then toil﴾, i.e., strive diligently in worship and exert yourself in gratitude for the blessings We have bestowed upon you in the past and for the favours We have promised you in the near future. It is also said: "So when you are free from your prayer, strive diligently in supplication." It is also said: "When you are free from your worldly affairs, toil in your prayer."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 94, verse 8:

﴿And to your Lord﴾ alone.

﴿So turn eagerly﴾ [to Him] with your requests, and do not ask anyone else, for He alone is able to grant your needs and no other is. It is also read "fa-raghghib" (فَرَغِّبْ), meaning: so make the people eager to seek what is with Him.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites "Alam nashrah" (ألَمْ نَشْرَحْ), it is as if he came to me while I was distressed, and then relieved me."
